definition: Multifarious means of many different kinds; highly varied.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word multifarious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know multifarious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandpa's multifarious toolbox held watch screwdrivers, fishing lures, sheet music, and a folding dentist's mirror.
Varied stops short of multifarious — a varied program has options, while a multifarious one seems to contain everything.
Kaleidoscopic goes further than multifarious — the variety is not just wide but shifting dazzlingly before your eyes.

Diverse says the members of a group genuinely differ from one another — a diverse committee, diverse habitats. Multifarious pushes the same idea toward astonishment: not just real differences, but so many different kinds at once that the sheer spread of the collection surprises you.

Assorted describes a modest mix of kinds gathered in one place — assorted chocolates, assorted screws in a jar. Multifarious operates at a grander scale: many genuinely different kinds at once, a range wide enough to startle. A drawer is assorted; a century-old general store is multifarious.

Multi- is everywhere in English — multiple, multitude, multiplex — but the word's other half, Latin -fariam ('in so many parts or ways'), survives in no other common word. Let the familiar multi- remind you of the meaning, and learn multifarious as its own word.
Multifarious means of many different kinds; highly varied.

The general store survived a century by stocking multifarious goods: snowshoes hung above canning jars, violin strings shared a drawer with fuse wire, and the storekeeper could produce a wedding veil or a wolf trap with equal speed.
Multifarious insists on more than number—'numerous' merely counts the items, while multifarious says the items are of genuinely different kinds, a range wide enough to surprise.
Multifarious is the formal, faintly admiring word for variety so wide it startles — duties, interests, collections.
For everyday range, 'varied' or 'all kinds of' is plainer; reach for multifarious when the sheer spread of kinds is the point of the sentence.

Every March, the transit authority publishes its annual inventory of items left behind on trains, and every March the city reads it aloud to itself in disbelief.

This year's list ran from the expected — 4,110 umbrellas, 900 single gloves — to a kettledrum, a taxidermied owl, a ball gown in its garment bag, and a terrarium of live crickets, rescued at the end of the northern line.
A columnist called the collection multifarious and meant it as a compliment: proof, she wrote, that no two riders carry the same life.
The clerk who runs the lost-property office was less romantic about the breadth of it.
'Everything people can own,' he sighed, 'they can also forget.'
